title: MaxDiff vs conjoint: how to choose the right method for your market research
summary: Choosing between MaxDiff and conjoint depends on the question you need answered. Compare outputs, sample sizes, and timelines, with worked examples of each.
body_markdown:
What is the difference between MaxDiff and conjoint analysis? +


MaxDiff asks people to choose the most and least preferred item from a small set. Across multiple sets, the results show which individual features, benefits, or messages people prefer and how far apart those preferences are. Conjoint asks people to choose between complete product concepts made up of multiple attributes. The statistical model shows each attribute's relative importance and how people trade one attribute for another. MaxDiff suits feature prioritization, while conjoint suits decisions about complete product offerings.


When should I use MaxDiff instead of conjoint? +


Use MaxDiff when your research objective is to prioritize individual items, and you need a clear ranking. It can help a product team determine which features matter most when deciding what to focus on. Use conjoint when the decision involves several product attributes together. For example, if you're deciding how price and pack size should work together in a new product, conjoint can show how consumers respond to those trade-offs and how different product combinations affect choice.


Can I run MaxDiff and conjoint in the same study? +


Yes, if your research objectives require both methods. MaxDiff can establish which individual features or benefits people prefer, while conjoint can show how those features affect choices when they appear together in a complete product. Running both adds more tasks to the study, which increases participant effort and can extend the timeline. Whether that makes sense depends on the decisions the research needs to support.


How many participants do I need for MaxDiff? +


A common starting point is around 300 participants per study, with at least 200 in each group you want to analyze separately, but no single sample size works for every study. The number you need depends partly on how many items you're testing and whether you need to analyze different groups separately. The aim is to collect enough data for the scores to remain stable and useful for the decision you're making.


How long does a MaxDiff study take? +


A MaxDiff study is usually quicker to set up than conjoint, because it only needs a list of items. Conjoint requires defining every attribute and option before launch, and each participant completes more tasks. For either method, the overall timeline mostly depends on recruitment. A hard-to-reach audience or several segments takes longer to fill.


How do I interpret MaxDiff scores? +


A MaxDiff score shows how strongly an item is preferred relative to the other items in the study. Higher scores indicate stronger preference, while the gap between scores shows how far apart items are. For example, scores of 26 and 24 suggest two items are close in preference, while scores of 26 and 10 show a much larger difference. When several scores cluster together, that can indicate a natural preference tier. However, the scores are quantitative data. They tell you what people prefer, but they don't explain why they made those choices.
